page: Google Cloud Platform n4a-standard-32 is a general-purpose virtual machine based on the Arm64 processor architecture. It provides 32 dedicated vCPUs along with 128 GB of system memory, matching a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-memory allocation ratio of 4.0 GB per core. The dedicated CPU configuration ensures consistent processor performance without resource sharing or credit depletion mechanisms typical of burstable tiers.

The instance does not include bundled local storage or integrated hardware accelerators, featuring zero local NVMe or SSD drives and no GPUs. All persistent storage must be provisioned independently via external network-attached volumes. Additionally, the instance provides zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses, requiring cloud routing or elastic network configurations for outbound or inbound Internet access.

From an architectural standpoint, the Arm-based profile delivers favorable price-to-performance efficiency for parallelized general-purpose compute loads compared to traditional x86 alternatives. Given its balanced resources and dedicated compute capacity, the n4a-standard-32 is appropriate for large web backends, container clusters, continuous integration pipelines, microservices fabrics, and distributed database nodes requiring moderate memory density.
description: Google Cloud Platform n4a-standard-32 is an Arm64-based general-purpose instance featuring 32 dedicated vCPUs and 128 GB of RAM, sustaining a 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio. Built on an efficient Arm architecture, it delivers predictable execution for workloads requiring steady-state performance across multiple cores. The instance does not include local disk storage or hardware accelerators such as GPUs, necessitating external network storage for persistent file systems and operating system disks. Furthermore, it includes no complimentary public IPv4 addresses. The hardware balance makes the n4a-standard-32 well-suited for cost-conscious, multi-threaded applications, including web application servers, containerized workloads, CI/CD runners, and distributed database services.
